The harp guitar is a string instrument built on the guitar: extra open strings that are not stopped and can be plucked individually are added to the guitar form, and at least one unstopped string lies outside the main fingerboard, normally played open. The family includes the American types with a hollow arm, a double neck or a frame carrying extra bass strings; the European bass guitar (contraguitar); and variants with high or middle floating strings, or several groups of floating strings. Players in Poland, Germany, Italy, Vienna and France used it, as did John McLaughlin, Michael Hedges, Robbie Robertson and Alfred Karnes and others, in ensemble work, concerts and film, and in old-time country and southern gospel recordings.
豎琴吉他的聲音特質來自吉他主體之外的一組或多組未按壓弦。這些弦通常不經指板按壓，: The sound of the harp guitar comes from one or more sets of unstopped strings beyond the guitar itself. These strings are usually not pressed on a fingerboard but plucked individually as open strings, so they ring on and can give a bass or middle-register drone and open chords in performance. The range is wider than an ordinary guitar's because of the extra strings, though the exact range varies with the form. Unlike an ordinary guitar, which changes pitch mainly by stopping strings, the harp guitar has at least one unstopped string outside the main fingerboard, keeping some pitches open and giving it a resonance clearly different from the rest of the family.
